literal: Prince of Anle, Prince of Guangchuan, Prince of Qi commandery, Prince of Hejian, Prince of Anfeng
idiomatic: The Princes of Anle, Guangchuan, Qi commandery, Hejian, and Anfeng

literal: Prince of Anle Changle, in the fourth year of Huangxing was enfeoffed Prince of Changchang, later changed to Prince of Anle.
idiomatic: Changle, Prince of Anle, was made Prince of Changchang in Huangxing year 4 and later transferred to Anle.

literal: Changle was by nature grave and steady; Xianzu valued and loved him.
idiomatic: Changle was sober and steady in temperament; Xianzu prized and favored him.

literal: In the first year of Chenming he was appointed Grand Commandant and sent out as Inspector of Ding Province.
idiomatic: In Chenming year 1 he became Grand Commandant and went out as Dingzhou inspector.

literal: He flogged powerful families and humiliated the gentry; many did not keep the law and were resented.
idiomatic: He lashed powerful clans and shamed the gentry; many broke the law under him, and he was widely hated.

literal: The common people went to the capital to sue him for his faults.
idiomatic: Commoners went to the capital to accuse him of misconduct.

literal: Gaozu punished him with thirty strokes of the staff.
idiomatic: Gaozu had him beaten thirty strokes with the staff.

literal: His greed and violence grew worse; for crime he was summoned to the capital.
idiomatic: His greed and brutality only deepened, until crimes brought him summoned to the capital.

literal: Later he and Inner-Steward Chief Yi Sihu plotted rebellion; when the affair broke out he was ordered to die at home.
idiomatic: Later he plotted treason with Inner-Steward Chief Yi Sihu; when it was exposed he was ordered to take his own life at home.

literal: He was buried with princely rites; posthumous title Li.
idiomatic: He was buried with princely honors and given the posthumous name Li (Fierce).

literal: His son Quan, style Souxian, inherited.
idiomatic: His son Quan, styled Souxian, succeeded to the title.

literal: At the beginning of Shizong's reign he was made Inspector of Liang Province.
idiomatic: Early in Shizong's reign he became Liangzhou inspector.

literal: In the province he was greedy and corrupt; government was accomplished by bribes.
idiomatic: In his province he was corrupt; office went to the highest bidder.

literal: Later he was removed and made Inspector of Ding Province.
idiomatic: He was later transferred to the Dingzhou inspectorate.

literal: When Prince of Jingzhao Yu rebelled, Yu falsely reported that the realm was in turmoil.
idiomatic: When Prince Yu of Jingzhao rose in rebellion, Yu spread false word of a dynastic crisis.

literal: The northern garrison provinces all suspected trouble at court and sent envoys to observe Quan's movements.
idiomatic: Northern border provinces suspected trouble at court and sent agents to watch Quan.

literal: Quan reported the full situation; the provinces and garrisons were settled.
idiomatic: Quan reported the facts in full, and the provinces and garrisons calmed.

literal: Yu fled to Xindu; Quan with Li Ping, Gao Zhi, and others attacked from four sides and set fires;[3] Yu burst through the gate and fled.
idiomatic: Yu fled to Xindu; Quan, Li Ping, Gao Zhi, and others besieged him from four sides and set fires;[3] Yu broke through the gate and escaped.

literal: Soon he was made Palace Attendant; for merit in being first to report, he was also made Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: Soon he was palace attendant; for being first to report the rebellion he was also made left vice director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: He died; posthumous title Wukang.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously titled Wukang.

literal: His son Jian, style Changwen, inherited.
idiomatic: His son Jian, styled Changwen, succeeded.

literal: Later he was made Inspector of Xiang Province and Grand Commander of the Northern Campaign to attack Ge Rong.
idiomatic: He was later made Xiangzhou inspector and grand commander of the northern campaign against Ge Rong.

literal: He still held concurrent office as Right Vice Director, Northern Route Mobile Office, and Director of the Masters of Writing; with Commissioner Pei Yan he jointly relieved Xindu.
idiomatic: He still held the right vice directorship, the northern route mobile office, and the directorship of the Masters of Writing, and with Commissioner Pei Yan relieved Xindu.

literal: Jian was a mediocrity; his younger brothers were violent and rough; seeing the realm in turmoil they plotted rebellion and surrendered to Ge Rong.
idiomatic: Jian was a mediocrity and his brothers violent; when the realm fell into chaos they plotted rebellion and went over to Ge Rong.

literal: Commissioner Yuan Ziyin with Pei Yan jointly besieged Jian; his head was sent to Luoyang; an edict changed their Yuan surname.
idiomatic: Commissioner Yuan Ziyin and Pei Yan jointly besieged Jian; his head was sent to Luoyang, and an edict stripped the clan of the surname Yuan.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Zhuang's reign restoration of the original clan was permitted; Jian's princely title was specially restored and he was posthumously made Minister of Works.
idiomatic: At Emperor Zhuang's accession the clan was allowed to resume its original name; Jian's princely title was specially restored and he was posthumously made Minister of Works.

literal: Jian's younger brother Binzhi, style Zishuang.
idiomatic: Jian's younger brother Binzhi, styled Zishuang.

literal: His nature was treacherous and without conduct; when he joined Jian in rebellion and was defeated, he fled to Ge Rong.
idiomatic: Treacherous and without principle, he joined Jian's rebellion; when it failed he fled to Ge Rong.

literal: When Ge Rong was destroyed he was able to return.
idiomatic: After Ge Rong's fall he was able to return.

literal: In the time of Emperor Chu he was enfeoffed Prince of Yingchuan commandery and entrusted with duties at the emperor's bosom.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Chu he was made Prince of Yingchuan commandery and given the emperor's innermost trust.

literal: When the emperor entered the Pass, Binzhi fled to Xiao Yan; later he returned to Chang'an.
idiomatic: When the emperor entered the Pass, Binzhi fled to Xiao Yan; he later returned to Chang'an.

literal: Prince of Guangchuan Lue, in the second year of Yanxing was enfeoffed.
idiomatic: Lue, Prince of Guangchuan, received his fief in Yanxing year 2.

literal: He held office as Grand Director of the Inner Palace; his nature was bright and keen, and in judging cases he was called fair.
idiomatic: He served as grand director of the inner palace; bright and keen by nature, he won a name for fairness in trials.

literal: In the fourth year of Taihe he died; posthumous title Zhuang.
idiomatic: He died in Taihe year 4 and was posthumously titled Zhuang.

literal: His son Xie, style Zhonghe, inherited.
idiomatic: His son Xie, styled Zhonghe, succeeded.

literal: In the nineteenth year he died.
idiomatic: He died in Taihe year 19.

literal: An edict said: "My imperial clan has known many losses; my younger cousin Xie has passed away, and grief cuts me so I cannot stop.
idiomatic: An edict read: "The imperial house has suffered too many losses; my cousin Xie is gone, and grief cuts so deep I cannot master it.

literal: In antiquity, for the mourning of great ministers there was the rite of three personal visits—this applied to those of the rank of the Three Excellencies and above.
idiomatic: In antiquity great ministers were mourned with three personal visits—a rite reserved for the Three Excellencies and above.

literal: As for ministers and offices below that, they should attend accordingly.
idiomatic: Ministers and offices below them were expected to attend in due measure.

literal: Since Han and downward the rite has largely been absent.
idiomatic: Since Han times the rite has largely fallen away.

literal: I wish to follow the ancient canon and let compassion follow feeling; though I lower myself by rank, private pain will not be eased.
idiomatic: I mean to follow the ancient canon and let compassion follow feeling; though rank demands restraint, private pain will not ease.

literal: I wish princes with kin in the period of mourning to make three visits, those of great-achievement kin to make two visits, and those of lesser-achievement and finest-mourning kin to make one visit.
idiomatic: I would have princes in the closest mourning circle pay three visits, those in the great-achievement circle two, and those in lesser or finest mourning one.

literal: The Prince of Guangchuan bears to me a great-achievement bond; I must certainly pay two visits.
idiomatic: Prince Guangchuan stands to me in the great-achievement circle; I shall certainly mourn him twice.

literal: The two visits mean: on the day of the great encoffment, to come in person and exhaust grief; after the mourning garments are complete, to go in finest hemp and offer condolence.
idiomatic: By two visits I mean: on the day of the great encoffment to come in person and exhaust grief, and after the mourning garments are complete to return in finest hemp and offer condolence.

literal: For finest-mourning kin after the encoffment there is no doubt in principle; as for the visit at the great encoffment—is it fitting or not?
idiomatic: Condolence in finest hemp after encoffment is plainly required; but is a visit at the great encoffment itself fitting?

literal: Must one comfort the bier at the first mourning, or should one exhaust grief at the closing of the coffin?
idiomatic: Should one comfort the bier at the first mourning, or exhaust grief only when the coffin is closed?

literal: As to whether early or late is proper, choose the mean between them.
idiomatic: Whether early or late is better—choose the mean."

literal: " Yellow Gate Attendant Cui Guang, Song Bian, Regular Attendant of Direct Transmission Liu Fang, Master of Ceremonies Lower Grandee Li Yuankai, Secretariat Attendant Gao Cong, and others deliberated:[4] "The matter of three visits is indeed an ancient rite; even through Han and Wei it has rarely been practiced.
idiomatic: Cui Guang and Song Bian of the Yellow Gate, Liu Fang, regular attendant of direct transmission, Li Yuankai, master of ceremonies lower grandee, Gao Cong, secretariat attendant, and others replied:[4] "Three visits are an ancient rite, yet from Han through Wei few have practiced it.

literal: Your Majesty is supremely sagely and benevolent and is about to follow the former track; your will must mourn the dead and your thought is the same as dwelling in the mourning hut.
idiomatic: Your Majesty is supremely sagely and benevolent and means to follow the former track; your will is true mourning, your heart the same as one dwelling in the mourning hut.

literal: We your subjects consider that if period kin make three visits, great-achievement kin should make two.
idiomatic: We hold that if the closest kin pay three visits, great-achievement kin should pay two.

literal: At the beginning of first mourning grief is at its utmost; since feeling has already lowered rank, one should follow the beginning of mourning.
idiomatic: At the beginning of mourning grief is at its height; since feeling has already bent rank, the first visit should fall at the beginning of mourning.

literal: As for the visit at the great encoffment, we bow to the sagely edict.
idiomatic: As for the visit at the great encoffment, we bow to Your Majesty's intent."

literal: An edict said: "Since Wei and Jin, personal visits have largely been wanting; for kin among ministers one necessarily wept in the Eastern Hall.
idiomatic: An edict said: "Since Wei and Jin, emperors have rarely mourned in person; for ministerial kin they wept in the Eastern Hall instead.

literal: Recently when Grand Marshal, Prince of Anding, died, after I had already visited him I again received condolences in the Eastern Hall; for today's affair, should I weep again?
idiomatic: When the Grand Marshal, Prince of Anding, died I visited him in person and still received condolences in the Eastern Hall; for today's rite, should I weep there again?"

literal: Guang and the others deliberated: "Weeping in the Eastern Hall was because one did not visit in person.
idiomatic: Guang and the others replied: "The Eastern Hall weeping existed because the emperor did not visit in person.

literal: Now Your Majesty in person comforts and views; the ministers follow the imperial carriage—we your subjects jointly consider that one should not weep again.
idiomatic: Now Your Majesty will comfort the bier in person and the ministers will follow your carriage—we hold there should be no second weeping."

literal: An edict said: "If the Grand Marshal is kin of weighty rank and position, one must weep in the Eastern Hall; yet Guangchuan is both a prince's son and still young in years and rank—you may deliberate as you will; I have no objection.
idiomatic: An edict said: "For the Grand Marshal, kin of the highest rank, the Eastern Hall is required; but Guangchuan is a prince's son and still young in years and station—deliberate as you see fit; I raise no objection."

literal: When Xie was about to undergo the great encoffment, Gaozu in plain white garments and deep mourning robes wept for him, entered the chamber, was stricken with grief, comforted the corpse, and went out.
idiomatic: On the eve of Xie's great encoffment Gaozu came in plain white and deep mourning, wept, entered the chamber, was overcome, comforted the corpse, and withdrew.

literal: The relevant office memorialized: the Princess of Guangchuan died in the capital of Dai; it is unclear whether the newly honored should follow the humbler old, or the humbler old should come to the newly honored.
idiomatic: The relevant office reported: the Princess of Guangchuan died in the Dai capital; it was unclear whether the newly honored dead should follow the humbler old, or the humbler old should be brought to the newly honored.

literal: An edict said: "For those who moved to Luoyang, from this time onward all may return their bones to Mount Mang; none may bury at the old tombs in Dai.
idiomatic: An edict said: "For families who moved to Luoyang, from now on all may rest their bones on Mount Mang; none may bury in the old Dai tombs.

literal: Where the husband was first buried in the north and the wife now dies in the south, the woman follows the husband and should be returned for burial in Dai;
idiomatic: If the husband was buried first in the north and the wife dies in the south, the wife follows the husband and should return to Dai for burial;

literal: if one wishes to move the father's grave to join the mother, that too may be done at will.
idiomatic: if one wishes to move the father's grave to the mother's side, that may also be done.

literal: Where the wife's tomb is in Dai and the husband dies in Luo, one may not let rank draw the lofty to the humble;
idiomatic: If the wife's tomb lies in Dai and the husband dies in Luoyang, rank may not draw the lofty down to the humble;

literal: if one wishes to move the mother to join the father, that should also be followed;
idiomatic: if one wishes to move the mother to the father, that should be allowed;

literal: if separate burial is desired, that too may be followed.
idiomatic: separate burial may also be chosen.

literal: If outside the burial limits, while the body lies in mourning in Dai, burial on either side may be done at will.
idiomatic: If the case falls outside these limits and the mourner is in Dai, burial on either side is at choice.

literal: Where household registers belong to Heng and Yan but office and person are in Jing and Luo, as to staying or leaving, that too follows choice.
idiomatic: Where registers remain in Heng and Yan but office and person are in Jing and Luo, staying or leaving is likewise at choice.

literal: Those attached to other provinces may each do as they wish.
idiomatic: Those attached to other provinces may each decide for themselves."

literal: An edict posthumously made Xie General of Martial Guard; posthumous title Gang.
idiomatic: An edict posthumously made Xie General of Martial Guard and gave him the posthumous name Gang.

literal: At the burial Gaozu in person attended and saw him off.
idiomatic: At the burial Gaozu attended in person to see him off.

literal: His son Lingdao inherited.
idiomatic: His son Lingdao succeeded.

literal: He died; posthumous title Prince Dao.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously titled Prince Dao.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: Chen, style Tanbao, was clever and quick as a child; Gaozu loved him.
idiomatic: Chen, styled Tanbao, was clever even as a child; Gaozu doted on him.

literal: In Shizong's time he was appointed Inspector of Ding Province.
idiomatic: Under Shizong he became Dingzhou inspector.

literal: Chen's consort was Shizong's maternal niece, younger sister of Empress Gao.
idiomatic: Chen's consort was Shizong's niece by marriage, the younger sister of Empress Gao.

literal: Chen relied on inside and outside connections and received many bribes; his greed knew no limit.
idiomatic: Chen leaned on court and family ties and took endless bribes; his greed had no bottom.

literal: When he returned to court, Empress Dowager Ling issued an edict: "At Dingzhou Chen failed only to carry off the Zhongshan Palace; otherwise there was nothing he would not seize—how can he be employed again?"
idiomatic: On his return Empress Dowager Ling edicted: "In Dingzhou Chen took everything but the Zhongshan Palace itself—how can he be used again?"

literal: Thereupon he was dismissed and kept at home.
idiomatic: He was thereupon dismissed and kept at home.

literal: When Suzong first began his studies, Chen presented a gilt-letter Classic of Filial Piety.
idiomatic: When Suzong first took up his studies, Chen presented a gilt-letter Classic of Filial Piety.

literal: Having no other way to advance, he became Liu Teng's adopted son and bribed Teng with gold and jewels numbering in the tens of thousands.
idiomatic: With no other path forward he became Liu Teng's adopted son and paid him bribes in gold and jewels beyond counting.

literal: Teng repeatedly spoke for him; he then obtained concurrent office as Director of the Court for the Imperial Clan and was sent out as Inspector of Qin Province.
idiomatic: Teng spoke for him again and again until he won the directorship of the Court for the Imperial Clan and went out as Qinzhou inspector.

literal: In the province he amassed wealth; the common people groaned.
idiomatic: In his province he amassed wealth while the people groaned.

literal: When the Di of Eastern Yi and Southern Qin rebelled, an edict made Chen Mobile Office and still charged him as Commissioner, returning him to oversee the province.
idiomatic: When the Di of Eastern Yi and Southern Qin rebelled, an edict named him to a mobile office and kept him as commissioner while he resumed the provincial post.

literal: Chen was by nature greedy and violent; holding both army and province he sought without end; the people suffered harm worse than from wolves and tigers.
idiomatic: Greedy and brutal by nature, he now held army and province together and took without end; the people suffered worse than from wolves.

literal: Advancing to attack the Di and Qiang, he suffered great defeat; a thousand soldiers died; he led the host in flight back.
idiomatic: He marched against the Di and Qiang and was shattered; a thousand soldiers died and he fled with the remnant.

literal: Relying within on Liu Teng, he feared nothing; the chief commandant impeached him; an amnesty came and he was stripped of name and made a commoner.
idiomatic: Backed by Liu Teng within, he feared nothing until the chief commandant impeached him; an amnesty spared his life but he was stripped of rank and made a commoner.

literal: Soon his princely title was restored; later in campaigning against Xianyu Xiuli he was defeated and stripped of office and title.
idiomatic: His princely title was soon restored; later, campaigning against Xianyu Xiuli, he was defeated and lost office and title.

literal: Later in campaigning against the Hu of Fen and Jin and the Shu, he died in the army; his princely title was posthumously restored.
idiomatic: Later, campaigning against the Hu of Fen and Jin and the Shu, he died on campaign; his princely title was posthumously restored.

literal: Prince of Anfeng Meng, style Jilie.
idiomatic: Meng, Prince of Anfeng, styled Jilie.

literal: In the fifth year of Taihe he was enfeoffed and made Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: In Taihe year 5 he received his fief and was made palace attendant.

literal: He was sent out as Grand General of Helong Garrison and Inspector of Ying Province.
idiomatic: He went out as grand general of Helong garrison and Yingzhou inspector.

literal: Meng was broad, benevolent, bold, and resolute, with great martial bearing; the frontier peoples feared and loved him.
idiomatic: Meng was broad, benevolent, bold, and resolute, with real martial presence; the frontier peoples both feared and loved him.

literal: He died in the province.
idiomatic: He died in his province.

literal: Posthumously made Grand Commandant; posthumous title Kuang.
idiomatic: He was posthumously made Grand Commandant and given the posthumous name Kuang.

literal: His son Yanming inherited.
idiomatic: His son Yanming succeeded.

literal: In Shizong's time he was appointed Grand Master of the Palace.
idiomatic: Under Shizong he was made grand master of the palace.

literal: At the beginning of Yanzhang, when the year brought great famine, Yanming then reduced his household wealth to save several dozen guests and also support their families.
idiomatic: Early in Yanzhang, in a year of great famine, Yanming spent his household wealth to save several dozen guests and support their families as well.

literal: By the beginning of Suzong's reign he was made Inspector of Yu Province and had great administrative achievements; he was repeatedly promoted to Attendant of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: At Suzong's accession he became Yuzhou inspector with a strong record of governance and rose to attendant of the yellow gate.

literal: Yanming had read exhaustively among the books and also possessed literary polish; he gathered more than ten thousand scrolls of maps and writings.
idiomatic: Yanming had read widely and wrote well; he collected more than ten thousand scrolls of maps and books.
